title: Cotton Candy Planets: Astronomers Find Two Super-Puffs in One System
summary:
What if a planet could be lighter than a carnival treat? Astronomers have found two Jupiter-sized exoplanets that are less dense than cotton candy. Named TOI-791 b and TOI-791 c, they orbit a Sun-like star about 1,113 light-years from Earth. They belong to a rare class called "super-puffs."

"Only a handful of these super-puffy planets are known, and it is even rarer to find two in the same system," said Dr. George Dransfield, who led the study. "Their extremely low densities make them fascinating targets for understanding how planetary systems form and evolve."

The first clues came from volunteers studying data from NASA's TESS space telescope. They noticed tiny dips in a star's brightness over time — signs that planets might be passing in front of it. To confirm, Dransfield's team used telescopes around the world. The ASTEP observatory in Antarctica was especially helpful: the continuous darkness of the Antarctic winter let them record several complete transits. Each transit — when a planet crosses in front of its star and blocks some light — lasted more than 11 hours. These were the longest complete planetary transits ever observed from the ground.

The team measured the planets' sizes by studying changes in the star's light during each transit. They calculated their masses by analyzing how their gravity affected each other's orbits. Together, these measurements showed extremely low-density worlds.

The two super-puffs orbit in a repeating pattern: for every five orbits the inner planet completes, the outer planet completes three. This suggests they formed together from the same disk of gas and dust around their star. The findings were published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society on June 25, 2026.

Scientists still aren't sure how super-puffs form. One leading theory is that they have large amounts of hydrogen and helium gas around small solid cores. These thick atmospheres would make the planets appear much larger than they really are while keeping their overall density extremely low. Dransfield's team hopes to solve the mystery by studying their atmospheres with the James Webb Space Telescope.
why_it_matters: Worlds this strange test the models scientists use to explain how every planetary system — including our own — is put together, and the discovery shows how volunteer data-checkers, telescopes on different continents and orbiting observatories can combine to find something no single team could.

background_read: Astronomers have now confirmed thousands of exoplanets — planets orbiting stars other than our Sun — and most were found indirectly, by watching a star's light dip. NASA's TESS space telescope (a planet-hunting observatory that scans the sky for exactly those tiny dips) has been supplying candidates since 2018, and volunteers often spot the most interesting ones first.

Density is simply mass divided by volume: Jupiter, our solar system's giant, is only about 1.3 times as dense as water, while real super-puffs are far lighter for their size — the famous ones in the Kepler-51 system were so light that astronomers re-checked the data before believing it.

Antarctica has long been a favourite home for telescopes, because the long polar night and very dry air give steady, uninterrupted views — the same reason the ASTEP observatory there could follow transits lasting more than 11 hours.
The results appeared in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, a journal published by a British astronomy society that has printed research for about two centuries.
The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, can read the chemistry of a planet's atmosphere — the tool Dransfield's team now hopes to use on these two worlds.

perspectives.description: Researchers see super-puffs as rare natural laboratories. Because only a handful are known, finding two around one star is a chance to test ideas about how gas giants grow and why some end up so puffy. The planned James Webb observations are the obvious next step.

Some scientists warn that low-density measurements are notoriously easy to get wrong — a slightly misjudged size or mass can make an ordinary planet look like a super-puff. Previous 'super-puff' claims have been re-examined, so independent confirmation with other telescopes matters.

The discovery fits a pattern: every new generation of planet-hunting telescopes turns up worlds our solar system doesn't have, such as hot Jupiters and now super-puffs. Each oddity forces astronomers to widen their theories rather than assume other systems look like ours.

The team's next goal is to use the James Webb Space Telescope to analyse starlight filtering through the planets' atmospheres, which could reveal what the thick envelopes are made of. If super-puffs really are gas shells around small rocky cores, that would reshape how we picture planet formation.
